title: The Albin Countergambit
description: A tricky response to the Queen's Gambit by White based on the central strike e5!?, leading to very fun positions. Sometimes, your opponent will lose in just 8 moves!

2k3r1/ppp1nRpp/2n5/4P3/2P5/4P2P/PP1Nb1P1.text:
Let's protect the g7-pawn.

White is left with all the weaknesses they had before, but fewer pieces to defend with.

Black is much better.

2k4r/ppp1nRpp/2n5/4P3/2P5/4P2P/PP1Nb1P1/.text: Even at the price of dropping another pawn.

2k4r/ppp1nppp/2n5/4P3/2P3b1/4P2P/PP1NB1P.text:
White accepts the temporary sacrifice...

But now we get two pieces for the rook.

Nine times out of ten, this is worth it.

2kr2nr/ppp2ppp/2n5/4Pb2/2P5/P4N2/1P3KPP/.text:
And we will castle, activating the rook as well.

Next, we will slowly build up our position until we eventually capture the e5-pawn.

Black is much better.

2kr3r/ppp1nppp/2n5/4P3/2P3b1/4PN1P/PP1NB.text:
White could nonchalantly play h3, thinking they simply attack your bishop.

But there's a tactic after this move.

We can capture on d2!

The white bishop is also under attack.

3rk1nr/ppp2ppp/2n5/4P3/2P3b1/4PN2/PP1N2P.text:
The knight comes out to e2 now, supporting the f3-knight.

We will still get the e5-pawn, though.

Because we can add an attacker to it with Nge7-g6.

And White is all out of defenders.

3rk2r/ppp1nppp/2n1b3/4P3/2P5/4PN1P/PP1N2.text:
Retreating to e6 and keeping the bishop is good because we also have to play on the light squares.

Next, our knight is coming to g6 and the e5-pawn will soon die.

3rk2r/ppp1nppp/2n5/4P3/2P3b1/4PN1P/PP1N2.text: We don't even have to take on f3 if White attacks the bishop.

r1b1k1nr/ppp1qppp/2n5/4P3/2P5/4PN2/PP1N2.text:
We can simply bring the queen to e7 and White can't save the e5-pawn.

We'll regain the material and maintain a much better pawn structure.

r1b1k1nr/ppp2ppp/2n5/4P3/1BP5/5N2/PP3pPP.text:
The king has to move again.

Finally, we'll recapture the bishop.

We went from being a pawn down to being a pawn up, and White has lost their castling rights.

Their e5-pawn is also isolated and weak.

They will get the f2-pawn back, but we will develop and castle in the meantime.

r1b1k1nr/ppp2ppp/2n5/4P3/2P5/P4N2/1P2KpP.text:
The king goes after the pawn.

It's great to see White making so many moves with the king and wasting time.

Meanwhile, we will develop. There is no need to rush with ...Bg4 and ...Nxe5.

The e5-pawn isn't going anywhere and castling is priority now.

r1b1k1nr/ppp2ppp/8/4P3/1nP5/P4N2/1P3pPP/.text:
White can attack our knight...

But we'll simply move to c6 and attack the pawn.

r1b1k2r/ppp1bppp/2n5/4P3/2P1N1n1/P3PN2/1.text: The bishop recaptures and White keeps castling rights.

r1b1k2r/ppp1bppp/2n5/4n3/2P1N3/P3PN2/1P4.text:
But the e5-pawn falls, and that's not the end of it.

The e3-pawn is still extremely weak and we haven't forgotten about it!

We will play against it next, already being better.

r1bqk1nr/ppp2ppp/2n5/4P3/1BP5/4pN2/PP3PP.text:
Taking the bishop on b4 instead of the pawn doesn't work.

White's move allows the capture on f2 with check.

r1bqk1nr/ppp2ppp/2n5/4P3/1BP5/5N2/PP2KpP.text:
The king has to slide to e2 to keep an eye on the queen.

We'll trade now.

r1bqk1nr/ppp2ppp/2n5/4P3/1bP5/4PN2/PP1B2.text:
If White wants to recapture on e3, they have to do so with the pawn.

Now, having damaged White's pawns, we are happy to exchange on d2.

r1bqk1nr/ppp2ppp/2n5/4P3/1bP5/4PN2/PP1N2.text:
White has no choice but to recapture, and look at their pawns now.

We are still down a pawn, but the doubled pawns on the e-file are simply waiting to be captured.

The knight can jump to both g4 and f5 from the h6-square, and we can include the queen  on e7 if we need to.

r1bqk1nr/ppp2ppp/2n5/4P3/1bPp4/4PN2/PP1B.text:
White will most likely block with the bishop here.

Don't capture the bishop as a reflex. The key move is taking the pawn on e3.

White's bishop is pinned for the moment so they can't recapture with it.

And both the bishop and the f2-pawn are under attack.

r1bqk1nr/ppp2ppp/2n5/4P3/1bPp4/4PN2/PP1N.text:
Blocking with the knight is less confrontational than blocking with the bishop, but it doesn't change our plans.

We will capture the pawn on e3.

r1bqk1nr/ppp2ppp/2n5/4P3/2P5/4PN2/PP1N2P.text: If the knight recaptures on d2...

r1bqk1nr/ppp2ppp/2n5/4P3/2P5/4PN2/PP1Q2P.text:
The queen recaptures.

The standard idea for Black in these variations of the Albin is playing against the weak e-pawns, and you have to keep this in mind at all times.

This is why we unleashed the ...Bb4+ and ...dxe3 maneuver in the first place.

Now the bishop activation to g4 targets the defender of the e5-pawn.

r1bqk2r/ppp1bppp/2n4n/4P3/2P5/P3PN2/1P1N.text:
White continues development.

They don't really have many ways of stopping our venture against the pawns.

We can fork both pawns now with Ng4.

White will surely lose one of them.

r1bqk2r/ppp1bppp/2n5/4P3/2P1N1n1/P3PN2/1.text:
They can protect the e3-pawn by centralizing the knight, and offer a queen trade.

But even a queenless middlegame works in our favor.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2n4n/4P3/1bP5/P3PN2/1P1N.text:
When White attacks our bishop, we don't have to trade for the knight. 

Bringing it back is fine.

White's weak pawns are on the dark squares so our bishop can only help.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/4P3/2Pp4/4PN2/PP3PP.text:
White challenges the pawn now and opens up the bishop.

This move is the most popular, and occurs in 25% of games in the database. 

They have to play this move at some point to continue development, so you can expect it.

We'll give a check on b4. This is a critical move and the gambit cannot work without it.

White can't block on c3 thanks to our d4-pawn and will therefore have to block on d2.

r2Qk1nr/ppp2ppp/2n5/4P3/2P3b1/4PN2/PP4PP.text:
White can also trade queens here.

We'll recapture with the rook.

This only helps our activity.

r2qk1nr/ppp2ppp/2n5/4P3/2P3b1/4PN2/PP1QB.text:
White defends.

We shouldn't rush and give up the bishop on f3 yet.

We can develop instead: a common idea is bringing our knight to g6 and putting more pressure on the e5-pawn.

r2qk2r/ppp1nppp/2n5/4P3/2P3b1/4PN2/PP1QB.text:
White could choose to castle here.

Having activated both knights, we can comfortably trade the queens.

r3k2r/ppp1nppp/2n5/4P3/2P3b1/4PN2/PP1NB1.text:
White recaptures.

We are fine with the queen trade. because we can now castle long and keep the momentum.

Apart from our knight arriving at g6, the h-rook is also coming to the center.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
The Queen's Gambit.

We will play ...e5, the Albin Countergambit!

We attack the center with another pawn and sacrifice the pawn on e5 for space and rapid development.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3pP3/2P5/8/PP2PPPP/RN.text:
If White wants to prove this gambit is dubious, they have to accept it.

And they will more than half the time, in 3.3 million games.

Our idea is to push the pawn to d4!

This pawn is protected and already restricts White's standard developing move: Nc3.

Apart from that, the e5-pawn and the c4-pawn are now split and the e5-pawn is already in our territory and vulnerable.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/4P3/2Pp4/5N2/PP2PPPP/.text:
Study 1 will deal with Nf3 on move 4.

White wants to attack the pawn first and then play e3 to challenge it.

This is played 70% of the time, far more frequently than 4.e3 which we will look in the next study.

There's only one natural move to protect the pawn, and that's ...Nc6.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the course on the Albin Countergambit!

This is a fun and powerful weapon against the Queen's gambit that may come as a big surprise to a lot of White players, especially those who mostly prepare with main lines.

It's characterized by ...e5 on move 2, potentially leading to extremely sharp and tactical lines that can easily pose problems for White.

White opens with d4, and we'll reply with d5.

r1b1k1nr/ppp2ppp/2n5/4P3/1bP1q3/4PNP1/PP.text:
It's best for White to develop and threaten a discovered attack on our queen.

We'll capture on e3 now, with check.

r1b1k1nr/ppp2ppp/2n5/4P3/1bP5/4qNP1/PP1N.text:
White blocks.

Our idea is to trade queens.

r1b1k1nr/ppp2ppp/2n5/4P3/1bP5/5NP1/PP1NK.text:
After the king recaptures, White has lost castling rights.

And that's not all.

r1b1k1nr/ppp2ppp/2n5/4P3/2P5/5NP1/PP1NB2.text:
We'll start doing that with ...Nc6.

As you already know, a common motif is bringing the other knight to g6 via e7 and harassing the e5-pawn.

As far as the light-squared bishop is concerned, we can both activate it to e6 or to h3 to pose some problems on the light squares.

It's more natural to castle long here.

r3k1nr/ppp2ppp/2n1b3/4P3/1bP5/5NP1/PP1NK.text:
White has even more weaknesses now, and the material is equal.

We'll develop the bishop and target the c4-pawn.

Apart from that, we can comfortably castle next move and bring the knight into the game.

We're better.

rn1qk1nr/ppp2ppp/8/4P3/1BP3b1/8/PP2K1PP/.text:
The point is that we have this check!

We will win the queen on the next move and the game is over.

rnb1k1nr/ppp2ppp/8/4P3/1BP4q/8/PP4PP/RN1.text:
We can bring the queen out to h4 with check.

White will have to move to d2 and they are simply busted.

rnb1k1nr/ppp2ppp/8/4P3/1bP1q3/4PNP1/PP1B.text:
White defends both with Nf3.

But we can trade on d2 now.

rnb1k1nr/ppp2ppp/8/4P3/1bP1q3/4PNP1/PP1N.text:
Once White develops and blocks the attack on the rook, we don't even have to rush capturing either pawn.

There is nothing White can do to defend them.

We can take a move here to develop the knight with Nc6 and put more pressure on the e5-pawn.

rnb1k1nr/ppp2ppp/8/4P3/1bP4q/4P1P1/PP1B3.text:
White blocks with the pawn, but we already know where our queen is going.

And that's the e4-square to attack the rook and the e3- and e5-pawns.

rnb1k1nr/ppp2ppp/8/4P3/1bP4q/4P1P1/PP1N3.text:
White will block with g3...

And we can slide the queen to e4.

Of course, it can't be captured by the knight because it's pinned.

Look at our active queen attacking the rook and both vulnerable pawns at the same time!

rnb1k1nr/ppp2ppp/8/4P3/2P1q3/4PNP1/PP1N3.text:
The knight has to recapture.

And we can win the pawn back, with check.

rnb1k1nr/ppp2ppp/8/4P3/2P5/4qNP1/PP1NQ2P.text:
White blocks with the queen.

Now trading is best.

rnb1k1nr/ppp2ppp/8/4P3/2P5/5NP1/PP1NB2P/.text:
The bishop recaptures.

And now it's time to continue development.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2ppp/8/4P3/1BP5/4p3/PP3PPP/R.text:
If White takes the hanging bishop, they are completely lost.

The reason is the following.

We will capture on f2 with a fork and the king mustn't recapture because of the hanging queen on d1.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2ppp/8/4P3/1BP5/8/PP2K1PP/RN.text:
White captures the knight, and we've gotten the piece back.

But that's not the point.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2ppp/8/4P3/1BP5/8/PP2KpPP/RN.text:
So White has to slide to e2.

Now if we take the knight and promote to a queen, White will be able to trade on d8 and then capture on g1.

We would regain the piece but the position would be equal. Do you see something better?

We can take on g1 and promote to...a knight!

This is crucial because it comes with check and White doesn't have time to take on d8.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2ppp/8/4P3/1BP5/8/PP4PP/RN1Q.text: Moving the king back to e1 doesn't help White's cause.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2ppp/8/4P3/1bP5/4P3/PP1B2PP/.text:
The only way for White to maintain some kind of equality is to recapture on e3.

But even then will we grab initiative.

The queen gives check! The dark diagonal has opened up and there is no knight on f3 to cover the h4-square.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2ppp/8/4P3/1bP5/4P3/PP1N2PP/.text:
White has to recapture, but this provokes other means of attack by us.

As in the main line, once we capture on e3 the h4-e1 diagonal opens up.

And we'll play Qh4+!

rnbqk1nr/ppp2ppp/8/4P3/1bPp4/4P3/PP1B1PP.text:
The critical line is White blocking with the bishop, of course.

We haven't played ...Nc6 this time, so our bishop isn't protected at all.

But we will still capture on e3!

rnbqk1nr/ppp2ppp/8/4P3/1bPp4/4P3/PP1N1PP.text:
You probably already know what to do if White blocks with the knight.

And that's to capture on e3.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White plays the Queen's Gambit.

We'll respond with the Albin Countergambit!

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3pP3/2P5/8/PP2PPPP/RN.text:
White accepts our gambit.

And it's important to push ...d4 here.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/4P3/2Pp4/4P3/PP3PPP/R.text:
The move e3 here could be considered a mistake, and it's played 12% of the time in more than 330,000 games!

It only goes to show that many people aren't prepared for the Albin.

As in the last study, we will give this check.

It will prove to be even more powerful now.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Study 2 of the first chapter will show us how to approach the position when White is impatient and plays the dubious 4.e3.

This premature move could easily be punished if White is not accurate, and in extremely entertaining ways at that!

Let's go, starting with White's 1.d4 and our reply of 1...d5.

2kr2nr/1pp2ppp/2n1b3/p3P3/2P2B2/P7/1P3PP.text: But we'll castle with the same ideas, with the added ...Nge7 and ...Ng6 maneuver to capture that weak e5-pawn.

2kr2nr/1pp2ppp/8/p3Pb2/2Pn4/P1N5/RP3PPP/.text:
And that's to dominate the e-file by placing the rook there after the knight maneuver.

We will probably capture the e5-pawn and even if we don't, we can challenge it with ...f6 since White's king is on the e-file.

Our knight is still eyeing those c2- and b3-squares.

r1b1k1nr/1pp2ppp/2n5/p3P3/2P5/P7/1P3PPP/.text:
White recaptures with the knight.

It's time to start targeting stuff.

The e5-pawn is hanging, and we'll attack the c4-pawn twice if we capture it.

On the other hand, the knight jumping to d4 and threatening a fork is also potent.

r1b1k1nr/1pp2ppp/2n5/p3P3/2PQ4/P7/1P3PPP.text:
Accepting the queen trade is already an inaccuracy.

We'll recapture, and our knight arrives at the d4-square where it is threatening to jump to the problematic light squares on c2 and b3.

r1b1k1nr/1pp2ppp/2n5/p3P3/2Pq4/P1N5/1P3P.text:
A better move than trading the queens is simply activating the knight to c3.

We'll trade queens anyway.

The d4-square being available for the knight is too tempting.

r1b1k1nr/1pp2ppp/8/p3P3/2Pn4/P7/RP3PPP/1.text:
Basically the only good move for White is Ra2, evading the forks.

Other moves like 10.Bd3 or 10.Kd1 lose on the spot!

We'll develop the bishop, and we are attacking the knight since the rook has moved.

r1b2rk1/1pp1nppp/2n5/p3P3/2PQ4/P7/1P2BPP.text:
White accepts.

We are happy to exchange queens because now the knight on d4 is a monster.

It's attacking the bishop on e2 and threatening to jump to c2 or b3.

r1b2rk1/1pp1nppp/8/p3P3/2Pn4/P7/1P3PPP/R.text:
Which is why White retreats and covers both squares.

But the bishop no longer protects the c4-pawn.

So we will attack it with Be6!

r1bq1rk1/1pp1nppp/2n5/p3P3/2PN4/P7/1P2BP.text:
White continuing to trade here will only give us more targets.

Let's offer to trade queens as well.

r1bq1rk1/1pp1nppp/2n5/p3P3/2Pb4/P1N2N2/1.text:
Again, White could abstain from trading.

Which is fine for us.

We'll take the knight and damage their pawn structure further.

r1bq1rk1/1pp2ppp/2n3n1/p3P3/2P5/P1P2N2/4.text:
And now White can't save the e5-pawn.

The c-pawns are also weak and clear targets.

r1bqk1nr/1pp2ppp/2n5/p1b1P3/2PP4/P4N2/1P.text:
Expect to see this trade as White wants to get rid of our problematic d4-pawn.

We'll recapture with the bishop, attacking the e5-pawn.

r1bqk1nr/1pp2ppp/2n5/p1b1P3/2Pp4/P3PN2/1.text:
White could also go the passive route and activate the bishop to e2.

In that case, we'll force them to capture in the center.

We'll play ...Bf5, threatening to push the pawn to d3.

r1bqk1nr/1pp2ppp/2n5/p3P3/2PN4/P7/1P3PPP.text:
White chooses to capture again.

We'll take with the queen, maintaining the attack on the e5-pawn.

White could easily go wrong here.

r1bqk1nr/1pp2ppp/2n5/p3P3/2Pb4/P4N2/1P2B.text:
We'll analyze Be2 here again as an alternative to trading in the center.

White may want to keep pieces on the board thinking they can get an advantage and castle.

We don't have to rush with capturing the e5-pawn and risking losing castling rights.

Let's bring the knight to e7 instead and castle on the next move.

r1bqk2r/1pp1nppp/2n5/p3P3/2Pb4/P4N2/1P2B.text:
White castles...

And so will we.

Now we intend capturing on e5 in the near future.

r1bqkbnr/1pp2ppp/2n5/p3P3/2Pp4/P3PN2/1P3.text:
In this study, White challenges the center with e3 and opens up the bishop.

This move is much better now that they have a pawn on a3.

It's played 40% of the time.

As mentioned, we'll bring the bishop to support the center.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/4P3/2Pp4/P4N2/1P2PP.text:
Which is why the most annoying line from White is 5.a3, played just over 20% of the time, in over 330,000 games.

White stops Bb4+, forcing us to change our plans.

So we'll stop any potential White b4 advance by playing a5. Then we'll bring our bishop to c5, supporting d4.

Apart from that, our ...Nge7 and ...Ng6 idea to target the e5-pawn is still viable.

Other ideas to mention here for Black are 5...f6 to develop rapidly, 5...Bg4, planning ...Qe7 and ...O-O-O, and 5...Nge7 to go for the e5-pawn.

r2qk1nr/1pp2ppp/2n5/p1b1Pb2/2PP4/P4N2/1P.text:
White basically has to take now.

The trades in the center will help us because of the vulnerable e5-pawn.

We'll recapture with the knight.

r3k1nr/1pp2ppp/2n1b3/p3P3/2P2B2/P7/1P3PP.text: White can defend the e5-pawn for now.

r3k1nr/1pp2ppp/8/p1b1Pb2/2Pq4/P7/1P2BPPP.text:
And I suggest we take with the queen here.

This is flexible because it attacks the e5-pawn and prepares queenside castling at the same time.

Black is doing fine here.

r3k1nr/1pp2ppp/8/p3Pb2/2Pn4/P1N5/RP3PPP/.text:
Of course, White will move it to c3.

But we have a concrete plan.

r4rk1/1pp1nppp/4b3/4P3/p1Pn4/PP6/5PPP/RN.text:
But not for long.

We'll challenge that structure right away and we've easily equalized.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
The Queen's Gambit.

We'll play the Albin.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3pP3/2P5/8/PP2PPPP/RN.text:
White accepts.

And we'll push the pawn to d4.

We already know that we want to give a check on b4 if White goes 4.Nf3 and 5.e3.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/4P3/2Pp4/5N2/PP2PPPP/.text:
White plays Nf3 first.

We'll defend the pawn.

Now ...Bb4+ is an idea.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
In Chapter 1 we saw that White can easily get in trouble if they aren't ready for our Albin Countergambit.

If we manage to push ...d4 and give a check on b4 we could already be in good shape.

However, when White knows what they're doing, they will prevent ...Bb4+ with a3 on move 5.

And that is what Chapter 2 is all about. Let's begin, with 1.d4 for White and our reply of 1...d5.

r1b1k2r/1pp1qppp/2n5/p3P3/2PN4/P7/1P2PPP.text:
The knight recaptures.

Now we'll castle.

White is currently up two pawns, but we have a big lead in development and are threatening to pin the knight with ...Rd8.

Also, the e5-pawn will soon fall.

r1b1k2r/1pp1qppp/2n5/p3Pn2/2PN4/P4N2/1P2.text:
And now the knight finally captures on d4.

White has captured the strong central pawn, but at what price?

We'll trade once.

r1b2rk1/1pp1qppp/2N5/p3P3/2P5/P7/1P2PPPP.text:
So, White trades on c6.

But they traded off their only active piece.

r1b2rk1/2p1qppp/2p5/p3P3/2P5/P7/1P2PPPP/.text:
We'll recapture, with easy ideas like ...Rd8 to attack the queen and ...Rb8 to pressure the queenside since our a-pawn is already restricting White from pushing. The e5-pawn is likely to fall shortly.

White is yet to activate their pieces and we are doing fine.

r1bQkb1r/1pp2ppp/2n5/p3Pn2/2P5/PN2pN2/1P.text:
White trades queens first.

The benefit for them is that we recapture with the king and lose the castling rights.

Our knight is too valuable on c6 to move it away.

r1bk1b1r/1pp2ppp/2n5/4Pn2/p1PN4/P3PN2/1P.text:
White can jump to the center in this line, having retaken control of d4.

We don't want to capture and fix their pawn structure.

Instead, developing the bishop and going for activity is better, even at the cost of ruining our pawn structure.

r1bk1b1r/1pp2ppp/2n5/p3Pn2/2P5/PN2PN2/1P.text:
And now the pawn recaptures.

White doesn't want to take with the bishop and let us have the bishop pair.

But we will play a4 and attack the knight on b3.

White captures.

White castles.

White has to recapture with the knight.

We can't really protect the d4-pawn now.

r1b1kb1r/ppp1qpp1/2n3n1/4P3/2Pp3p/5N1P/P.text:
And the main target is of course the e5-pawn.

We already have two knights on it and if needed will add the rook as an attacker on h5.

r1b1kr2/ppp1q1pp/8/8/2PNn3/4Q3/PP2PPPP/R.text:
The queen doesn't have many squares to go to.

White certainly can't stop us from playing Qb4+.

It is an important move because White has to move the king and keep it weak and in the center.

r1b1kr2/ppp1q2p/2n5/6p1/2Ppn3/PN3N1P/1P2.text: They go for h3 instead to prevent ...g4.

r1bqk2r/ppp3pp/2n2n2/8/1bPp4/1N3N2/PP1BP.text:
White blocks with the bishop.

We'll trade.

r1bqk2r/ppp3pp/2n2n2/8/2Pp4/1N3N2/PP1QPP.text:
The queen comes to d2, and our pawn is still under attack.

Let's centralize the knight and attack the queen, though.

r1bqk2r/ppp3pp/2n5/8/2PpnQ2/1N3N2/PP2PPP.text:
White doesn't have time to capture, so slides the queen to f4...

In this position, we are giving away the d4-pawn. But our play is on the b4-square, where we want to place our queen, therefore we'll play Qe7, also defending our knight.

White has to be careful because the most natural moves lose the game on the spot.

r1bqkb1r/ppp1nppp/2n5/4P3/2Pp1B2/5N2/PP1.text:
White can't do much to stop this, so they activate the knight.

And we'll fork the bishop and the pawn.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2pp1/2n3n1/4P2p/2Pp3P/5NB1/P.text:
White could block our advance with h4.

We'll just continue attacking the e5-pawn.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2pp1/2n3n1/4P2p/2Pp4/5NBP/PP.text:
The one that gives us space is h3.

We will still attack the bishop with h4.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n3n1/4P3/2Pp4/5NB1/PP1.text:
White retreats to g3.

Do you remember our ideas from the chapter on 5.a3?

We'll push the h-pawn and hope to trap the bishop!

White basically has two ways to deal with this.

r1bqkb1r/ppp3pp/2n2n2/8/2Pp4/1N3N2/PP2PP.text:
White goes for the attack on the pawn.

When this happens, your main ideas should revolve around giving a check on the b4-square.

This will force White to block with the bishop which will actually give life to our position in the long run.

r1bqkb1r/ppp3pp/2n2n2/8/2Pp4/5NP1/PP1NPP.text:
White could also go for the fianchetto here, and in this case we'll go for a familiar idea.

We'll bring out our light-squared bishop and set up a battery.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/4P3/2Pp1B2/5N2/PP2P.text:
White going for 5.Bf4 will lead to similar plans for us as in the 5.a3 and 6.Bf4 lines we looked at.

This is played 10% of the time in almost 200,000 games.

It definitely provokes the ...Nge7 idea from us, aiming for the g6-square.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/4P3/2Pp4/5N2/PP1NPP.text:
A move that's played equally as often as 5.Bf4 is White developing the knight to d2.

The knight might want to come to b3 quickly and attack our pawn.

So I suggest we act immediately and challenge the center in gambit spirit!

This will accelerate our development and provide enough resources for a battle in the center.

An alternative was ...Nge7.

r1bqkbnr/ppp3pp/2n2P2/8/2Pp4/5N2/PP1NPPP.text:
White captures, naturally.

We'll take back with the knight.

r2qkb1r/ppp3pp/2n2n2/5b2/2Pp4/5NP1/PP1NP.text:
White develops the bishop.

And we will line up our queen and bishop.

r3kb1r/ppp1qpp1/2n3n1/4Pb1p/2Pp3P/1N3NB1.text:
What we can do is activate the bishop and prepare long castling if White captures on d4.

Also, the queen is coming to b4 with check so White does have to be careful here.

r3kr2/ppp3pp/8/5b2/1qPNn3/4Q3/PP2PPPP/R2.text:
And we are easily winning after ...Bf5.

The bishop protects the knight and we will castle on the next move, bringing the rook to the dangerous d-file.

White will not be able to defend.

r3kr2/pppbq2p/2n5/6p1/2Ppn3/PN3N1P/1P2PP.text:
But our bishop can simply develop to d7, and we will castle on the next move.

White's king is extremely weak and their position is passive.

In fact, Black is winning!

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
The Queen's Gambit.

Let's go for the Albin.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3pP3/2P5/8/PP2PPPP/RN.text:
White captures...

And we'll push, of course.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/4P3/2Pp4/5N2/PP2PPPP/.text:
The knight comes out.

And we'll protect the pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
In Chapter 4 of the Albin Countergambit, we will look at some fifth move deviations by White.

Instead of 5.a3 or the 4.Nf3/ 5.e3 setups, White can choose some other options to try to counter our Albin aggression.

You will see a lot of familiar motifs in this chapter.

Study 1 will deal with 5.Bf4 and 5.Nbd2. Let's begin with 1.d4 d5.

2kr1b1r/ppp3p1/2n2q1p/5b2/2Pp4/5NP1/PP2P.text:
And we'll do the same, but on the opposite side of the board.

We've got the bishop pair and a clear plan to attack on the kingside with moves such as ...g5 and ...h5.

r1b1k2r/ppp3p1/2n2q1p/8/1bPP4/5N2/PP1N1P.text:
When White captures in the center, we shouldn't rush recapturing.

There could be Qa4+ ideas.

r1b1kb1r/ppp3p1/2n2q1p/8/2Pp4/5N2/PP1NPP.text:
We can just recapture with the queen, and there are no issues in the position.

The bishop is coming to f5 and we'll castle.

Standard.

r1b1kb1r/ppp3p1/2n2q1p/8/2Pp4/5NP1/PP2PP.text:
White goes for kingside development.

We'll bring our bishop is out to f5, the most active square.

r1bqk2r/ppp3b1/2n2n1p/6p1/2Pp4/1N3NB1/PP.text: White finally jumps to b3 and attacks the d4-pawn...

r1bqk2r/ppp3b1/2n4p/6p1/2Ppn3/1N3NB1/PP2.text:
But we can centralize the knight and attack the active bishop on g3.

We've got three pieces defending the pawn.

If White plays e3, you can capture and even accept the queen trade.

The b2-pawn will be hanging.

Apart from that, White is struggling to find ideas.

r1bqk2r/ppp3p1/2n2B1p/8/1bPp4/4PN2/PP1N1.text:
White can force our hand by capturing.

However, they give up the valuable bishop.

We'll capture and activate our queen.

r1bqk2r/ppp3p1/2n2n1p/8/1bPp3B/4PN2/PP1N.text:
Retreating to h4 doesn't help.

We'll continue chasing the bishop.

r1bqk2r/ppp3pp/2n2n2/6B1/1bPp4/4PN2/PP1N.text:
Now the knight has to block.

It is different, however, because if we take on e3 the bishop on g5 can recapture.

Which is one of the benefits of White having played 5.Bg5.

That's why we will attack the bishop.

r1bqk2r/ppp5/2n2n1p/6p1/1bP5/4PNB1/PP1N2.text: The f-pawn recaptures and it's now extremely weak.

r1bqk2r/ppp5/2n2n1p/6p1/1bPp4/4PNB1/PP1N.text:
White retreats to g3.

And we'll now capture on e3.

There is no bishop to recapture and therefore White ends up with a weak central pawn.

r1bqkb1r/ppp3p1/2n2B1p/8/2Pp4/5NP1/PP2PP.text:
So White captures on f6.

And our queen gets out.

We will follow simple development from here and castle long.

r1bqkb1r/ppp3p1/2n2n1p/8/2Pp3B/5N2/PP1NP.text:
White retreating to h4 poses a question.

Do we want to play ...g5 or is it too weakening for the kingside?

The answer is that we do!

We can use this maneuver to fianchetto on g7.

Convenient.

r1bqkb1r/ppp3pp/2n2B2/8/2Pp4/5N2/PP2PPPP.text:
This capture is actually pretty common, played 25% of the time.

White doesn't want any complications but simply gets rid of our knight.

We'll recapture, activating our queen.

r1bqkb1r/ppp3pp/2n2n2/6B1/2Pp4/4PN2/PP3P.text:
White challenging our pawn now happens a quarter of the time.

It's an inaccuracy for a reason we are already familiar with.

White has done nothing about the b4-square.

So we'll give a check there.

r1bqkb1r/ppp3pp/2n2n2/6B1/2Pp4/5N2/PP1NP.text:
White develops the knight here 20% of the time.

The knight wants to jump to the b3-square and attack our pawn.

We'll grab a tempo and attack the bishop.

r1bqkb1r/ppp3pp/2n2n2/6B1/2Pp4/5NP1/PP2P.text:
Expect to see the fianchetto here 10% of the time.

White seems content with the trade on f6 and wants to develop calmly.

Now the bishop doesn't have the retreating h4-square when we attack it.

r1bqkb1r/ppp5/2n2n1p/6p1/2Pp4/5NB1/PP1NP.text:
White retreats to g3...

And we develop the bishop.

It will act as an effective defender of the d4-pawn.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/4P1B1/2Pp4/5N2/PP2P.text:
And White goes for this aggressive move 9% of the time.

Obviously, our queen is under attack and we can't move it to a useful square.

We have to block. I recommend ...f6!

We offer a trade of pawns, but we open the e- and the f-file and speed up our development.

This is a sharper response than ...Nge7 and might catch White off guard.

r1bqkbnr/ppp3pp/2n2P2/6B1/2Pp4/5N2/PP2PP.text:
White captures.

Let's recapture with the knight.

r2qk2r/ppp5/2n2n1p/5bp1/1bP5/4PNB1/PP1N2.text:
We'll simply finish development and attack the pawn with ...Qe7 next.

Our king is going to castle queenside.

Black is better because of the strong bishops and the clear target on e3 which we will organize our attack towards.

r3k2r/ppp3p1/2n2q1p/8/1bPP2b1/5N2/PP1N1P.text:
Instead, we can pin the defender of the pawn and prepare castling.

No matter what, our rooks are coming to the center and we are in great shape.

White probably won't save the pawn on d4.

r3kb1r/ppp3pp/2n2q2/5b2/2Pp4/5N2/PP1NPPP.text:
We have a straightforward plan. We'll castle long and push the g-pawn to attack the knight.

We've got much more space than White and their setup has left their pieces stuck together.

Black is definitely better here.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
Two pawns in the center.

We'll play the Albin.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3pP3/2P5/8/PP2PPPP/RN.text:
White takes.

We'll push forward with d4.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/4P3/2Pp4/5N2/PP2PPPP/.text:
Attacking the pawn.

We'll develop, defending it.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Study 2 will show us how to approach 5.Bg5 by White on move 5.

Using their pawn on e5, White wants to put pressure on our queen early and provoke a trade, disrupting our development.

Let's see what the antidote is. We'll begin with 1.d4 d5.

3rkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/8/2b5/2N5/PP1BPPPP/.text:
And we'll develop the knight to f6.

We've equalized in material and have most of our pieces out.

If White plays e4, you can trade the light-squared bishops.

If we trade light-squared bishops on f1, we also have the plan of Nb4 and Nd3+.

3rkbnr/ppB2ppp/2n5/8/2b5/2N5/PP2PPPP/R3K.text:
White captures.

And it's better to keep the rook on the d-file than sliding it to c8, since we're preventing White from castling.

3rkbnr/ppp2ppp/2n1b3/8/2P2B2/2N5/PP2PPPP.text:
A move that looks more active than Bd2 is Bf4.

White is not going to castle yet and gives up the c4-pawn.

However, the bishop is attacking c7.

Let's take the pawn anyway.

We'll be able to attack the white bishop and keep developing faster.

3rkbnr/ppp2ppp/2n1b3/8/2P5/2N1P3/PP3PPP/.text:
And even more surprisingly, the move that is the most popular and played a third of the time loses for the exact same reason.

White defends the c4-pawn but overlooks our other threat.

I expect you will win a bunch of games like this!

The knight has the b4-square! White can't stop the check on c2 now.

3rkbnr/ppp2ppp/2n1b3/8/2P5/2N5/PP1BPPPP/.text:
White could go for the passive-looking Bd2, with the intention of castling queenside quickly.

The bishop is blocking the d-file.

Let's just capture the free pawn.

3rkbnr/ppp2ppp/4b3/8/1nP5/2N1P3/PP3PPP/1.text:
The best they can do is move the rook so that they don't get forked.

We'll give the check anyway.

3rkbnr/ppp2ppp/4b3/8/2P5/2N1P3/PPn1KPPP/.text: The king has to slide to e2, and now the c4-pawn is up for grabs.

3rkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/8/2b5/2N1P3/PPn1KPPP/1R.text:
And we'll take it with check.

White has to move to f3 after which we will win the bishop on f1.

This is completely winning for Black.

4kbnr/pp1r1ppp/2n5/8/2b2B2/2N5/PP2PPPP/R.text:
And when White goes back to f4...

We can threaten a fork on c2!

4kbnr/pp1r1ppp/8/8/1nb2B2/2N5/PP2PPPP/2R.text:
White has to stop it with the rook.

But that loses the pawn on a2.

4kbnr/pp1r1ppp/8/8/5B2/8/bP2PPPP/2R1KBNR.text:
And we'll recapture.

Although we've won back the pawn, there's a lot of chess to be played.

A smart idea would be to try and give a check on b4 since White's king is completely restricted.

Apart from that, our knight is coming to the natural f6-square.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/3Q4/2P5/2N5/PP2PPPP.text:
Very rarely does White abstain from capturing on d5.

We don't want to trade queens here and activate their knight.

We can continue attacking the queen instead with Be6.

For the price of a pawn, we already have two pieces developed with tempo.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/3p4/2P5/2N5/PP2PPPP.text: Retreating to d1 is too passive and gives us what we want.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/8/2Pp4/2N5/PP2PPPP/.text:
And that's to push the pawn.

Now there are no problems in the position and we are simply better.

r2Qkbnr/ppp2ppp/2n1b3/8/2P5/2N5/PP2PPPP/.text:
White will most likely capture here.

We'll recapture with the rook and we've got a lot of potential in the position.

Our knight would love to reach the c2-square from either d4 or b4.

Meanwhile, the c4-pawn is under attack.

Keep in mind that 7.Nf3 loses on the spot due to ...Nb4, and it's the second most popular move!

rnb1kb1r/pp3p1p/2p2n2/q5N1/2Pp1N2/8/PP2P.text: We have a fork on a5 and we will win the knight.

rnbqkb1r/pp3p1p/2p2n2/4N3/2Pp2p1/3N4/PP2.text:
White jumps to the center, but the knight can only be a target there.

In fact, the knight on e5 doesn't have any free squares now.

rnbqkb1r/pp3p1p/2p2n2/6N1/2Pp1N2/8/PP2PP.text: Capturing on g5 loses to a tactic.

rnbqkb1r/pp3p1p/2p2n2/6p1/2Pp4/3N1N2/PP2.text:
The best move for White is to retreat to d3.

But we can continue chasing their pieces with g4.

This is a good idea because it completely disrupts White's developing plans, while giving us space on the kingside.

rnbqkb1r/pp3p1p/2p5/4N3/2Ppn1p1/3N4/PP2P.text:
This centralizing move is important to remember because we are threatening ...Qa5+ to trade everything off.

If that happens, we will have ...f6 to trap the knight!

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p2n2/8/2Pp1N2/5N2/PP2PP.text:
White activates the other knight.

Now there's two attackers on the d4-pawn.

We can continue in a calmer manner and develop while defending, but I suggest a sharper plan.

How should we continue?

We can play ...g5!

Sacrificing the pawn, we attack the knight one more time.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/2p5/8/2Pp1N2/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
And that's f4.

Before we continue to chase the knight, it's important to develop.

We also take away the potential h5-square from the knight this way.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
The Queen's Gambit.

We'll play the Albin.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3N4/2Pp4/8/PP2PPPP/R1.text:
Taking with the knight on d5 is only played 8% of the time, and for a reason.

White's knight is oddly placed on d5 and will get kicked around.

We'll start attacking it with ...c6.

Already, there's only one square the knight can jump to.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3p4/2PQ4/2N5/PP2PPPP/.text:
By far the most common move, played 88% of the time, is White recapturing on d4 with the queen.

This seems logical because there is immense pressure on the d5-pawn now.

In fact, we can't really defend it.

What we can do is develop with tempo and gambit the pawn this way.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3pp3/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPPP.text:
And now the knight comes out on move 3. It's played just over 20% of the time in almost 2 million games.

White doesn't capture either pawn, but rather reinforces the attack on the d5-pawn.

They might prefer capturing it with the knight.

When this happens, it's usually a good idea to capture the d4-pawn.

If White doesn't want to take, we will!

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Chapter 5 of our Albin course will show what happens when White  doesn't accept the gambit pawn on move 3!

This usually shows that White isn't prepared to go into the aggressive lines of the gambit and wants a calmer game.

Study 1 will deal with 3.Nc3.

We'll begin with White's 1.d4 and our reply of 1...d5.

3rkbnr/ppp1qppp/8/5b2/1nP5/N3PN2/PP3PPP/.text:
We can continue improving while grabbing tempi with ...Rd8 here, attacking the queen.

White will have to move the queen again and we can continue with logical developing moves like ...Nf6, as well as activating the dark-squared bishop.

We can also contemplate ...Nd3+ in some variations to get White's light-squared bishop. ...c6 is also good to defend b7.

r1b1kbnr/ppp1qppp/2n5/3Q4/2P5/4PN2/PP3PP.text:
Let's demonstrate how we can extract the most out of the position.

We will both attack the queen and threaten a fork on c2.

r1b1kbnr/ppp1qppp/8/8/1nP5/4PN2/PP3PPP/R.text:
This forces the queen back into passivity.

Let's renew the threat of the fork by playing Bf5.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/3Q4/2P5/4P3/PP3PPP/.text:
Once White captures on d5, I suggest avoiding the trade, although that is playable as well.

I think it's better to slide the queen to e7.

We want to leave the White queen on d5 and make it a target with moves like ...Nf6 and ...Nb4.

Also, our light-squared bishop is coming to either e6 or f5 to help out.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/8/1bBP2b1/2N1BN2/P.text: White defends with the bishop for now.

r3kbnr/ppp1qppp/8/5b2/1nP5/N3PN2/PP3PPP/.text: While we are developing in the optimal way, White has to defend with moves like Na3.

r4rk1/ppp2ppp/2nq1n2/8/1bBP2b1/2N1BN2/PP.text:
But we aren't done yet.

A good plan now is to bring the rook to the d-file to support the queen.

Also, rather than capturing the c3-knight, the bishop would be much more useful on b6 from where it would attack the pawn.

rn1q1rk1/ppp2ppp/5n2/8/1bBP2b1/2N2N2/PP3.text:
White castles...

And now we'll bring the knight to c6, with the concept of taking on f3 and then d4.

We've activated both queenside pieces in the last two moves and already managed to create a threat on the isolated pawn.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2ppp/5n2/3p4/1bPP4/2N2N2/PP2.text:
White will probably play Be2 rather than capture on d5.

In that case, we can take on c4 and make them move the bishop again!

We gain a tempo this way.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2ppp/5n2/8/1bBP4/2N2N2/PP3PP.text:
White captures.

They now have an IQP on d4 which is automatically our primary target.

How will we approach it?

Well, we will pin its defender first.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3p4/1bPP4/2N2N2/PP3P.text:
White continues development...

And we'll castle, focusing on queenside development next.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3p4/2PP4/2N5/PP3PPP.text:
White's knight on c3 does a good job controlling the center and especially the d5-square.

Which is why we will pin it.

Not necessarily to capture it, just to restrict it.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
The Queen's Gambit.

We'll go for the Albin.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3p4/2PP4/8/PP3PPP/RNB.text:
White will recapture with the pawn almost three quarters of the time.

It makes sense to keep the pawns in the center.

This line will be a lot more peaceful than the usual Albin variations, but that's okay.

Every gambit has a positional side, too.

When there are no tricks or potential for immediate aggression, it's important to develop optimally.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3p4/2PQ4/4P3/PP3PPP/R.text:
The queen recapturing will get White another pawn, but will give us a lot of freedom and activity.

It's played around 20% of the time.

We'll attack the queen first, gambiting the d-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3pp3/2PP4/4P3/PP3PPP/.text:
It definitely seems like White is scared when they play this move.

It is usually suboptimal to defend this early when you're facing a gambit.

The move 3.e3 is played 13% of the time in more than 1.2 million games.

Let's take on d4.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Study 2 will focus on 3.e3 by White.

It is a passive move, but could lead to a solid setup by White and normal development by both sides without much confrontation early.

That is what White wants when they play e3, but it also shows the flexibility of the Albin that Black can get a good position even without fireworks on the board!

We'll begin with 1.d4 d5.

r1b1k1nr/pp3ppp/n7/1Np5/8/8/PP1KPPPP/R4B.text: The knight can jump back to b5...

r1b1k1nr/ppp2ppp/2n5/3q4/1Q1Pp3/2N2N2/PP.text:
Now White has a cunning continuation where they actually capture the bishop.

Now our queen is under attack, since the pin has been eliminated.

But this is just a fancy way to trade pieces, and we capture the queen.

r1b1k1nr/ppp2ppp/8/3N4/1n1Pp3/5N2/PP2PPP.text:
White captures our queen.

White is threatening a fork as well as us, so it doesn't pay off to jump into c2.

We'll get the piece back instead.

The knight is still under attack on f3.

r1b1k1nr/ppp2ppp/8/3nN3/3Pp3/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White jumps to the center.

Before we develop, we could improve one of our pieces and reintroduce a threat.

Nb4 is useful because White has to react to the threat of Nc2+ again.

r1b1k1nr/ppp2ppp/8/4N3/1n1Pp3/8/PP2PPPP/.text:
And with the king, too!

Now it's finally time to continue development.

r1b1k1nr/ppp2ppp/n7/8/1b1N4/8/PP1BPPPP/R.text:
The only way White can block now is with the bishop on d2.

A trade is fine for us.

r1b1k1nr/ppp2ppp/n7/8/3N4/8/PP1KPPPP/R4B.text:
White recaptures with the king.

Losing castling rights isn't as much of a factor here, because the queens have been traded.

Let's continue expanding, while attacking White's misplaced knight.

r1b1kb1r/ppp1nppp/2n5/4P3/8/5N2/PP2PPPP/.text:
We can bring the knight to e7 from where it will jump to g6.

Our bishop is coming to either of the three squares that are e6, f5 or g4, and we'll castle long.

We already have a nice position and jare likely to win the pawn on e5 back.

r1b1kbnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/3q4/3P4/5N2/PP3PPP/.text:
White defends.

You probably already know the next move.

It's pinning the knight on f3.

r1b1kbnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/4P3/8/5N2/PP2PPPP/R.text: White defends, but we already know the common Albin ideas that we can implement here as well.

r1b1kbnr/ppp2ppp/n7/8/3N4/8/PP2PPPP/R1B1.text:
White captures in the center now.

But we can develop with tempo as well.

Why not give a check on b4 when the knight has ventured away?

r3k1nr/p1p2ppp/2p5/8/1bqP4/2N5/PP2QPPP/R.text:
The best way for White to get out of trouble is force a queen trade.

We have to take.

r3k1nr/pp3ppp/n3b3/1Np5/8/8/PP1KPPPP/R4B.text:
But we are well protected and there's easy development to come.

We don't even have to castle. Placing the knight on f6 and the king on e7 is safe enough.

Our rooks will probably come to the center quicker than White's.

r3k1nr/ppp2ppp/2B5/8/1bqP4/2N5/PP3PPP/R1.text:
White captures with check first.

We'll recapture with the pawn to keep the queen on c4.

r3k1nr/ppp2ppp/2n5/3q4/1b1P2b1/2N2N2/PP2.text:
White blocks with the knight, which is also pinned now.

Our idea was to attract the knight to c3 and only then capture on f3.

Why?

r3k1nr/ppp2ppp/2n5/3q4/1b1P4/2N2B2/PP3PP.text:
Well, once the bishop recaptures we can place the queen on c4 and prevent castling!

This could be dangerous for White, especially if they let us castle and bring the rook to the e-file.

Also, the knight on c3 is under attack twice.

r3k1nr/ppp2ppp/4b3/4N3/1n1Pp3/8/PP2PPPP/.text:
It's important to activate the bishop to e6 first.

This is designed so that we have ...Bb3+ if White plays a3, which would give us a big advantage with ...Nc2 coming after it.

Apart from that, ...f6 is good to kick away White's only active piece and our flexible knight can develop to e7.

r3k2r/p1p1nppp/2p5/8/1b1P4/2N5/PP2KPPP/R.text:
But we keep the same ideas.

The pawn on d4 is still isolated and weak and we'll target it with ...Nf5.

We will still castle long and our rooks are coming to the center.

r3kbnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/3q4/3P2b1/5N2/PP2BPPP.text:
White defends.

Don't rush and capture on f3 and then on d4.

That would lose the queen after Bxc6+!

We can give a check on b4 instead.

r3kbnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/8/3P2b1/5N2/PP3PPP/RN.text:
But we will attack it with our bishop.

There are also ideas of ...Nb4 to threaten the fork, and we will castle queenside, of course.

The pawn on d4 is still vulnerable.

rnb1k1nr/p1p3pp/5p2/1p1qN3/Q2Pp3/2P5/P3P.text:
We'll just block with the pawn and now the queen is attacked as well.

This is completely winning for Black.

rnb1k1nr/pp4pp/2p1qp2/4N3/Q1PPp3/8/P3PPP.text:
But they won't be saving the knight after ...c6.

We will be winning a piece.

rnb1k1nr/ppp2ppp/6q1/8/1b2N3/4P3/PP1N1PP.text:
And our queen is safe and strong on g6, actually restricting White's bishop from developing comfortably.

Also, the knight on e4 is currently under attack because its defender is pinned.

Our knights will come out next, with a lively position to come.

rnb1k1nr/ppp2ppp/8/3q4/1b1Pp3/2N5/PP1NPP.text:
A much safer move than Ne5 is Nd2.

It turns out that White didn't have many options for the knight after all.

This gives us the d4-pawn but attacks the e4-pawn.

rnb1k1nr/ppp2ppp/8/3q4/Qb1Pp3/2N2N2/PP2P.text:
White could force our hand and go for the check on a4 immediately, trying to exploit the position of our bishop on b4.

But we are the only ones who have the potential to come out on top in this line.

We'll block with the knight and defend the bishop.

rnb1k1nr/ppp2ppp/8/3qN3/1b1Pp3/2N5/PP2PP.text:
White could just blitz out Ne5 here, seeing that their knight is under attack and thinking that e5 is the most active square.

In fact, this is the most common move.

But it's a mistake.

Let's capture on c3 first to neutralize any Qa4+ ideas.

rnb1k1nr/ppp2ppp/8/3qN3/3Pp3/2P5/P3PPPP/.text:
Why was Ne5 a mistake?

Well, after f6 the knight is trapped!

rnb1k1nr/ppp2ppp/8/8/1b1qp3/2N1P3/PP1N1P.text:
First of all, White can use the chance to play e3 with tempo, attacking our queen.

I recommend the d6-square, even though our queen will be attacked again on the next move.

We will transfer it to the kingside.

rnb1k1nr/ppp3pp/4qp2/4N3/Q1PPp3/8/P3PPPP.text: White can try the check on a4.

rnb1k1nr/ppp3pp/5p2/3qN3/2PPp3/8/P3PPPP/.text:
White's best effort to keep fighting is c4, attacking the queen.

But we can simply slide to e6.

As long as the knight is still trapped, we're good.

rnb1k1nr/ppp3pp/5p2/3qN3/Q2Pp3/2P5/P3PPP.text: If White gives this check now, it's even worse.

rnb1kbnr/ppp2ppp/8/1N6/3p4/8/PP2PPPP/R1B.text:
The knight comes to b5 and threatens both a fork as well as the d4-pawn.

Unfortunately, we can't defend both.

We will defend against the greater threat on c7, of course.

rnb1kbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3q4/3P4/8/PP3PPP/RNBQ.text:
And we have created an IQP with this trade, which could prove to be a downside for White.

In any case, it makes our position easy to play.

We will just harass the pawn as much as possible, starting by developing with Nc6.

rnb1kbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3q4/3Pp3/2N2N2/PP2PPP.text:
White has an intermezzo with Nc3.

It would be great for them if we just passively moved the queen away.

But we have the Bb4 pin, which is also the best move.

rnb1kbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3q4/3Q4/4P3/PP3PPP/RN.text:
If the queen recaptures, our ideas of harassing the IQP will stay the same, just without the queens.

We'll accept the trade.

rnb1kbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3qP3/8/8/PP2PPPP/RNBQ.text:
Taking on e5 now doesn't make a whole lot of sense.

It's played just under 20% of the time.

We'll accept the queen trade and ensure White loses castling rights. White has not played the opening very positively.

rnb1kbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3qp3/3P4/2N5/PP2PPPP/.text:
The most common move is Nc3 here, attacking the queen, and it's played a third of the time.

However, White gives up the d4-pawn!

We will gladly capture.

Let's see their idea.

rnb1kbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3qp3/3P4/4P3/PP3PPP/R.text:
White chooses to protect the center with a pawn over 20% of the time.

Let's isolate their pawn by capturing on d4.

rnb1kbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3qp3/3P4/5N2/PP2PPPP/.text:
A move that's played 27% of the time is Nf3.

It feels the most natural to protect the center before attacking our queen with Nc3.

The e5-pawn is also under pressure.

So we don't have many options but to push and attack the knight back.

rnb1kbnr/ppp2ppp/8/4P3/8/8/PP2PPPP/RNBK1.text:
White recaptures.

And now we can attack the pawn with Nc6.

rnb1kbnr/ppp2ppp/8/4p3/3Q4/2N5/PP2PPPP/R.text:
Firstly, they want to trade the queens.

And after we recapture...

rnb1kbnr/ppp2ppp/8/8/3P4/8/PP3PPP/RNB1KB.text:
White takes, and now the pawn is isolated again.

Let's attack it immediately whilst also developing.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
The Queen's Gambit.

Let's play the Albin.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3Pp3/3P4/8/PP2PPPP/RN.text:
White captures on d5 13% of the time, in almost 1.2 million games.

Their idea is to leave the tension between the pawns on e5 and d4 but attract our queen to the center, so that they can get some developing moves with tempo before they take on e5.

We will still recapture with the queen, attacking the d4-pawn.

White has a lot of options here.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
We've mostly considered White taking the pawn on e5 after the Albin, as that is the offered pawn.

But what if White takes the pawn on d5 instead?

This leads into a whole new world of theory which we will explore in the final study of this chapter.

We'll begin with 1.d4 and our reply of 1...d5.
